text:
Cuts to disability benefits are likely to increase the risks of destitution faced by young people and leave millions of people unable to regularly afford everyday basics such as food, shelter and clothing, according to new research.
Destitution is “becoming the norm” with about 3.8 million people, including 1 million children, experiencing the most extreme form of financial hardship in the UK last year, says the Joseph Rowntree Foundation.
A quarter of people in destitution had no income at all, while a further 58% reported net incomes after paying rent of less than £90 a week, the research found, with those affected increasingly reliant on crisis services such as food banks.
Although the research was completed before the recent Milburn report’s proposals to scrap disability benefits for under-25s, it notes the current low rates of benefits mean young people are already at disproportionately high risk of destitution.
The government is to publish a white paper in the new year setting out its responses to the Milburn report, as well as Tuesday’s expected Timms review of the main disability benefit, personal independence payment (Pip).
Disability campaigners and poverty charities have made it clear they will oppose any attempts to remove disability benefits for under-25s, arguing that financial insecurity has a negative impact on health and makes it harder for people to get a job.
People are defined as destitute if they have been unable to afford two or more of the six basic necessities over the past month: shelter (ie, not sleeping rough); food; heating; lighting; clothing and footwear; and basic toiletries.
The destitution research, by academics at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh, said historically Pip – which supports people with the extra costs of disability – played a “critical role” in helping disabled people to escape extreme financial hardship.
“It is therefore imperative that any future changes to benefits following the Timms and Milburn reviews should ensure that disability benefits reach people with health conditions and/or disabilities with the greatest need for additional financial support, and without undue delay,” the report says.
“This is especially important for disabled people whose income is so low that they risk destitution,” it adds.
It notes that halving universal credit health payments in April to all new claimants was likely to “significantly reduce the incomes of some households at risk of destitution”. Last week the Milburn review recommended this benefit be removed for all under-25s.
About 61% of destitute people report a disability or long-term health condition, and while the public debate centres on increased numbers of people claiming disability benefits, the research found 37% of destitute people with life-limiting conditions were not receiving disability benefits.
“What is particularly disturbing is the evidence that destitution is becoming a more persistent experience, with people repeatedly needing crisis support simply to meet their basic needs,” said the report co-author Prof Suzanne Fitzpatrick of Heriot-Watt University.
“We are no longer looking at a temporary spike in hardship. Millions of people remain unable to afford the basic necessities needed to live, and there is something profoundly wrong when that becomes an enduring feature of life for so many in the UK.”
Greater London had the highest rate of extreme hardship, with two in every 100 households experiencing destitution. The UK local authority areas most affected were Newham, Westminster, Manchester, Tower Hamlets and Hounslow.
Groups most likely to experience destitution were single working-age adults, disabled people, people from minoritised ethnic communities, and migrants.
“Without action, we risk destitution becoming the norm for millions in the UK. Behind these stark figures are real people who don’t have what they need to survive – food, shelter, basic toiletries and clothing,” said Julian Hartley, the group chief executive of the Joseph Rowntree Foundation.
A government spokesperson said: “This government is turning the tide on poverty after years of rising hardship. Household incomes have risen 5% in real terms, food bank usage has fallen and the decision to remove the two-child limit will lift 450,000 children out of poverty by the end of this parliament.”
“We will consider the findings of the Milburn and Timms reviews together and set out the next steps on our reforms in the coming weeks, but we are clear that there will always be a strong safety net for those who need it.”
